manifest.title: Nagura's Theorem and the Interesting Numbers

inputs.abstract:
This submission formalizes Jitsuro Nagura's 1952 theorem that every natural
number $x \ge 25$ has a prime $r$ with $x < r < 6x/5$. It then applies that
theorem to classify the "interesting numbers" from
[mathlib4 issue #6091, item 91](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/issues/6091):
the only natural numbers satisfying the stated neighboring-prime
factorization condition are $14$ and $21$.

The analytic argument is combined with explicit, kernel-checked prime chains
below $5{,}000{,}000$. The complete proof was produced with substantial
language-model assistance. OpenAI Codex performed the decisive proof
development and integration; Leanstral was used in earlier exploratory and
module-level attempts; Anthropic Claude independently audited the resulting
source and verification evidence. The publisher does not claim personal
authorship or independent expert understanding of the proof.

concepts.title: Classification of Interesting Numbers
concepts.description:
Let $n$ be interesting when there are distinct primes $p$ and $q$ such that
$n=pq$, and when replacing $p$ by its next prime and $q$ by its previous prime
gives a factorization of $n+1$. Then $n$ is interesting exactly when
$n=14$ or $n=21$.

The two factors are existentially labelled. This is equivalent to the
opposite labelling used in mathlib4 issue #6091 because multiplication is
commutative.
concepts.sourceText:
import Mathlib

/-!
---
title: Classification of Interesting Numbers
type: theorem
---
Let $n$ be interesting when there are distinct primes $p$ and $q$ such that
$n=pq$, and when replacing $p$ by its next prime and $q$ by its previous prime
gives a factorization of $n+1$. Then $n$ is interesting exactly when
$n=14$ or $n=21$.

The two factors are existentially labelled. This is equivalent to the
opposite labelling used in mathlib4 issue #6091 because multiplication is
commutative.
-/

namespace Lax59.InterestingNumbers

/-- The number called `pNext` is the first prime strictly after `p`. -/
def NextPrime (p pNext : ℕ) : Prop :=
  pNext.Prime ∧ p < pNext ∧ ∀ r, r.Prime → p < r → pNext ≤ r

/-- The number called `qPrev` is the last prime strictly before `q`. -/
def PrevPrime (qPrev q : ℕ) : Prop :=
  qPrev.Prime ∧ qPrev < q ∧ ∀ r, r.Prime → r < q → r ≤ qPrev

/-- The neighboring-prime factorization property from issue #6091. -/
def Interesting (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ p q pNext qPrev : ℕ,
    p.Prime ∧ q.Prime ∧ p ≠ q ∧
    NextPrime p pNext ∧ PrevPrime qPrev q ∧
    n = p * q ∧ n + 1 = pNext * qPrev

/-- Exactly 14 and 21 satisfy the interesting-number property. -/
axiom interesting_iff (n : ℕ) : Interesting n ↔ n = 14 ∨ n = 21

end Lax59.InterestingNumbers

statements.signature: interesting_iff : ∀ (n : Nat), Iff (Lax59.InterestingNumbers.Interesting n) (Or (Eq n 14) (Eq n 21))
statements.doc: Exactly 14 and 21 satisfy the interesting-number property.

concepts.title: Nagura's Prime Interval Theorem
concepts.description:
For every natural number $x \ge 25$, there is a prime natural number $r$
strictly between $x$ and $6x/5$. The inequality is encoded without division as
$5r < 6x$.
concepts.sourceText:
import Mathlib

/-!
---
title: Nagura's Prime Interval Theorem
type: theorem
---
For every natural number $x \ge 25$, there is a prime natural number $r$
strictly between $x$ and $6x/5$. The inequality is encoded without division as
$5r < 6x$.
-/

namespace Lax59.Nagura

/-- The natural-number form of Nagura's prime-interval property. -/
def NaguraBound : Prop :=
  ∀ x : ℕ, 25 ≤ x → ∃ r : ℕ, r.Prime ∧ x < r ∧ 5 * r < 6 * x

/-- Nagura's theorem in the natural-number form used by this submission. -/
axiom nagura_bound : NaguraBound

end Lax59.Nagura
